items: Apply walks the same DAG the plan produced.
Calls `ApplyResourceChange` per node in dependency order.
State is written incrementally as each resource completes.
Partial success is a normal outcome, not corruption.
Nothing is rolled back; no cross-resource atomicity exists.
Recovery is always: re-run `plan`, read what work remains.
Design configurations so a re-run after failure is safe.
If the state write itself fails, `errored.tfstate` is dumped.

lines: terraform plan   # confirm what is left

items: Raising parallelism multiplies 429 and quota errors.
Per-resource `timeouts` override slow provider defaults.
Plan runtime scales with resource count via refresh.
The structural fix is smaller root modules, not faster flags.

blocks.title: Must Match
items: Same Terraform version.
Same provider versions.
The plan artifact itself.
An unchanged state serial.
`-auto-approve` is fine in CI when the plan was reviewed.
On a laptop it is how databases die.
Concurrent applies on one state are the top corruption risk.
Locking is the only guard — never make `-lock=false` routine.

blocks.title: Outside The Model
blocks.text: `local-exec` runs outside plan and state: it cannot be planned, diffed or retried safely. Prefer `user_data` or cloud-init.

items: The provider normalizes JSON whitespace, tag case, ARN casing.
Config never matches state, so the diff never empties.
Fix with `jsonencode()` on policy documents.
Or `ignore_changes` for attributes you do not own.
`force-unlock` on a live apply corrupts shared state fastest.
Stale saved plan? Re-plan; never work around it.
Committing `tfplan` or `terraform.tfstate` leaks secrets.
Both are plaintext, and git keeps them forever.
`depends_on` overuse: every extra edge serializes the graph.
Prefer real attribute references and let the graph infer.
Mutually referencing security groups create a cycle.
Split them into standalone rule resources.

lines: # removing list[1] shifts every later index

items: Removing a middle element replaces everything after it.
Switching `count` to `for_each` destroys the whole set.
Add `moved` blocks to keep identity across the switch.
Skimming past `# forces replacement` on a stateful resource.
Ignoring drift, so your apply reverts a console hotfix.
Treating the plan as a guarantee.
`(known after apply)` can resolve to something the API rejects.

blocks.title: Same Versions Both Sides
blocks.text: Plan and apply on different Terraform or provider versions means the applied diff is not the diff anyone reviewed.

blocks.title: `prevent_destroy`
items: Forgotten on production data stores.
Then surprising when it blocks a legitimate `-replace`.
Set it deliberately and document the removal path.
Applying a saved plan is the only reviewed-equals-applied path.
`-detailed-exitcode`: 0 no changes, 1 error, 2 changes.
That is the drift-detection gate in CI.
Automate review, not approval.
`(known after apply)` marks an unknown value.
`# forces replacement` names the attribute that triggered it.
Drift lives in `Objects have changed outside of Terraform`.
Accept it with `terraform apply -refresh-only`.
Edges come from references first.
`depends_on` only for invisible runtime dependencies.
Cycles are config bugs — decompose the mutual references.
`-target` includes deps, excludes dependents, warns loudly.

blocks.title: Speed Costs
items: `-refresh=false` costs accuracy.
`-target` costs completeness.
`-parallelism` costs rate limits.
Structure beats all three.

blocks.title: No Rollback
blocks.text: Apply has no cross-resource atomicity; state is written incrementally and re-running the plan is the recovery path.

a_bullets: Apply it twice in a row.
The second plan must say `No changes.`
Gate CI on unexpected `delete` actions in the JSON plan.
